```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from coreforecast.scalers import boxcox, boxcox_lambda

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
beer = D.beer()
souvenirs = D.souvenirs()
lynx = D.lynx()
noise = D.white_noise(n=len(spine), seed=7,
                     start=str(spine["ds"].iloc[0].date()))

_stl_raw = STL(spine["y"].to_numpy(), period=12, robust=True).fit()
trend_only = spine.assign(y=np.asarray(_stl_raw.trend))

# The seasonal panel is decomposed on logs: on the raw scale the swing grows with
# the level (about fivefold over 37 years), so "seasonality only" came out as noise with
# a variance break instead of a repeating shape.
_stl_log = STL(np.log(spine["y"].to_numpy()), period=12, robust=True).fit()
season_only = spine.assign(y=np.asarray(_stl_log.seasonal))
```

## Eyeballing cannot be tested, and does not scale

::: {.notes}
Pick up from where we stopped: just before the exercise, the subseries plot could not
show the spine's seasonality underneath a sixfold trend. That was not a bad plot, it is
the limit of looking.
:::

Describing patterns by eye has a wider problem:

::: {.incremental}
- **Does not scale**: impossible across hundreds of series
- **Subjective**: different people see different patterns
- **No significance test**: cannot tell signal from noise
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Solution
Replace guesswork with **numerical diagnostics**: ACF, STL decomposition, and feature summaries.
:::

# A. Autocorrelation {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 2.8–2.9 · The central diagnostic

## ACF is correlation with your own past

Quantifies linear correlation between $y_t$ and its lag $y_{t-k}$:

$$r_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t - \bar{y})(y_{t-k} - \bar{y})}{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t - \bar{y})^2}$$

::: {.incremental}
- **$r_k \in [-1, 1]$**
- **$r_1$** $\rightarrow$ correlation with previous month (inertia/trend)
- **$r_{12}$** $\rightarrow$ correlation with same month last year (seasonality)
- Plot $r_k$ against $k$ and you have a **correlogram**, the ACF plot
:::

::: {.notes}
If you have ever done a scatterplot of x against y, you have done this. The only
new thing is that x and y are the same column, offset by k.
:::

## A lag plot on a trending series only shows the trend

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
detrended = spine["y"].to_numpy() - P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 4.4))
P.lag_plot_grid(spine["y"], lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[0])
P.lag_plot_grid(pd.Series(detrended).dropna(), lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[1])
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("raw turnover ($M)", size=10)
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("trend removed ($M)", size=10)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine())
# Detrended with a 12-month centred moving average:
detrended = spine["y"].to_numpy() - P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(10, 4.4))
P.lag_plot_grid(spine["y"], lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[0])
P.lag_plot_grid(pd.Series(detrended).dropna(), lags=(1, 6, 12), axes=axes[1])
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("raw turnover ($M)", size=10)
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("trend removed ($M)", size=10)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Raw (top): every lag scores $r \approx 0.98$, which is the trend talking
- Trend removed (bottom): lag 12 jumps to $0.73$, lag 6 turns **negative**
:::

::: {.notes}
The trend is removed here with a 12-month moving average, which is segment 4. Do not teach it yet. The point is only that the raw lag plot cannot separate the two.
:::

## Bounds separate real correlation from luck

**White noise**: no autocorrelation at any lag, every value independent of every
other. For such a series:

$$r_k \sim N\left(0,\ \tfrac{1}{T}\right)$$

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- 95% of autocorrelations fall inside **$\pm 1.96/\sqrt{T}$**
- A spike inside the bounds is indistinguishable from noise
- With 36 lags, ~1–2 spikes outside the bounds can occur by chance
:::

## Slow decay: the spine ACF is dominated by trend

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
P.acf_plot(spine["y"], nlags=36, ax=ax, highlight_every=12, ylim=(-0.15, 1.05),
           title="Spine ACF, 36 lags (annual lags in orange)")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
P.acf_plot(spine["y"], nlags=36, ax=ax, highlight_every=12, ylim=(-0.15, 1.05),
           title="Spine ACF, 36 lags (annual lags in orange)")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Every lag sits far outside the bounds and decays slowly, which is trend
- The annual lags (orange) are **not** spikes here: the trend swamps them
:::


::: {.notes}
Ask why lag 12 is not a spike here when the seasonal plot was so obvious. Answer:
every lag is already near 0.9 because of trend, so seasonality has no room left to
show. Removing the trend is what the next segment does.
:::

:::


::: {.notes}
The first two panels were split out with STL, which is segment 4. Do not teach it
yet. Read the figure column by column: top row is the series, bottom row is its
ACF. The claim is only that each component leaves a different shape, and that you
can go the other way. That is exactly what Exercise 1.3 asks for.
:::

## Reading any ACF in five shapes

| Visual Pattern | Underlying Property |
|---|---|
| Slow, smooth decay | **Trend** |
| Repeating peaks at $m, 2m, 3m$ | **Seasonality** (period $m$) |
| Decay + Seasonal peaks | **Trend + Seasonality** |
| All spikes inside bounds | **White Noise** (no remaining signal) |
| Slow oscillating wave | **Cycle** (no fixed period) |

. . .

::: {.cardbox .teal}
**Key application**: When model residuals are white noise, the model has captured all systematic structure.
:::

# B. Decomposition {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 3 · Separating trend, season, and noise

## Box-Cox flattens the growing swing

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
lam = boxcox_lambda(spine["y"].to_numpy(), method="loglik")
yt = boxcox(spine["y"].to_numpy(), lam)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0], title="Original: expanding swing",
              ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.plot_series(spine.assign(y=yt), ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE,
              ylabel="transformed turnover",
              title=rf"Box-Cox ($\lambda = {lam:.2f}$): constant swing")
P.thin_xticks(axes, n=4)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine())
# Box-Cox transformation with optimal log-likelihood lambda:
lam = boxcox_lambda(spine["y"].to_numpy(), method="loglik")
yt = boxcox(spine["y"].to_numpy(), lam)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
P.plot_series(spine, ax=axes[0], title="Original: expanding swing", ylabel="turnover ($M)")
P.plot_series(spine.assign(y=yt), ax=axes[1], color=P.ORANGE,
              ylabel="transformed turnover", title=rf"Box-Cox ($\lambda = {lam:.2f}$): constant swing")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- When swing grows with level, transform before decomposing
- $\lambda \approx 0 \implies$ Use a standard **log transform** ($\log y_t$)
- Forecasting on it? Back-transforming returns the **median**, not the mean (Ch 5.6)
:::


::: {.notes}
Lambda came out near zero, which is the log case. Worth saying that Box-Cox is a
family with the log at one end, not a separate technique. Everything after this slide
in the segment runs on the transformed series. The median-vs-mean point is the
one they will trip over in production: if a regional total is the sum of 40
back-transformed store forecasts, that total is biased low unless you correct it.
:::

## A centred moving average estimates the trend-cycle

$$\hat{T}_t = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} y_{t+j} \qquad (m = 2k + 1)$$

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.2))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"3-MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 3),
            "12-month MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)},
    ax=ax, tail=180, colors=[P.PINK, P.ORANGE], ylabel="turnover ($M)",
    title="Spine, last 15 years: the order $m$ decides what survives")
P.thin_xticks(ax, n=5)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine(), last 15 years / 180 obs)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.2))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"3-MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 3),
            "12-month MA": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)},
    ax=ax, tail=180, colors=[P.PINK, P.ORANGE], ylabel="turnover ($M)",
    title="Spine, last 15 years: the order $m$ decides what survives")
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Set the window to one seasonal period: $m = 3$ keeps the season,
$m = 12$ erases it.
:::

::: {.notes}
The 3-MA still wobbles because three months is a quarter of a cycle, so it averages
a high month with two lower ones and keeps the shape. Twelve covers every month
once. Twelve is even and has no middle month, which is the wrinkle the next slide
deals with, so do not use the name 2x12-MA yet.
:::

## A whole-cycle window cancels the season

Averaging $m = 2k+1$ terms of $y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$, centred on $t$:

$$\hat{T}_t = \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} T_{t+j}}_{\text{trend}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} S_{t+j}}_{\text{season}}
            + \underbrace{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=-k}^{k} R_{t+j}}_{\text{noise}}$$

::: {.incremental}
- **Season $= 0$, exactly**: the window spans one whole cycle
- **Trend survives**: a symmetric window is unbiased on a linear trend
- **Noise shrinks** by $1/m$, damped but never removed
:::

::: {.notes}
Take the middle term first. One full cycle of a seasonal component sums to zero by
definition, and the window is exactly one cycle, so that term is not small, it is zero.
The trend term: with $T_{t+j}$ locally linear the symmetric offsets cancel and you get
$T_t$ back. Everything left over is damped noise. That is the whole argument, and it is
worth saying slowly because the rest of the segment rests on it.
:::

## An even $m$ needs the 2×$m$-MA to stay centred {.smaller}

Twelve months have **no middle month**: their average sits at $t + \tfrac{1}{2}$. Average two adjacent 12-MAs to land back on $t$:

$$\hat{T}_t = \tfrac{1}{24}y_{t-6} + \tfrac{1}{12}\sum_{j=-5}^{5} y_{t+j}
              + \tfrac{1}{24}y_{t+6}$$

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 7.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 1.7))
P.ma_weight_plot(12, ax=ax, title="13 weights, symmetric about $t$")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# 2x12 Centred Moving Average filter weights:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 1.7))
P.ma_weight_plot(12, ax=ax, title="13 weights, symmetric about $t$")
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
$y_{t-6}$ and $y_{t+6}$ are the **same calendar month**, so between them it still gets $\tfrac{1}{12}$, like every other month. The season cancels exactly.
:::


::: {.notes}
The two half weights land on the same calendar month, six months either side of t.
Between them that month still gets a full 1/12, like every other month, so the season
still cancels exactly. That is the only reason the 2x12 form exists.
:::

## Classical decomposition is averages all the way down

::: {.incremental}
1. $\hat{T}_t$ is the 2×12-MA
2. Detrend: $y_t - \hat{T}_t$
3. $\hat{S}$ averages the detrended values within each month, then centres them to sum to zero
4. $\hat{R}_t = y_t - \hat{T}_t - \hat{S}_t$
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Every piece is a moving average or a group mean. No fitting, no parameters. That simplicity costs something.
:::


::: {.notes}
No fitting, no parameters, nothing to tune. That is its appeal and also its ceiling,
which the next slide shows.
:::

## The MA trend stops six months short of the present

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.3))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"2×12-MA trend": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)},
    ax=ax, tail=60, colors=[P.ORANGE], shade_gap="2×12-MA trend",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)", title="Spine, last 5 years")
P.thin_xticks(ax, n=5)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian retail takeaway turnover (spine = D.spine(), last 5 years / 60 obs)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.3))
P.trend_overlay_plot(
    spine, {"2×12-MA trend": P.centred_ma(spine["y"], 12)},
    ax=ax, tail=60, colors=[P.ORANGE], shade_gap="2×12-MA trend",
    ylabel="turnover ($M)", title="Spine, last 5 years")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- The first and last $m/2$ observations get no trend estimate
- The missing one is exactly where you forecast from
:::

::: {.notes}
The other cost of classical decomposition: monthly means impose one seasonal shape on all
37 years. STL, next, fixes both problems at once.
:::

## STL (Seasonal-Trend using Loess) splits all three

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
res = STL(yt, period=12, robust=True).fit()
dcmp = spine.assign(
    **{"transformed turnover": yt},
    trend=np.asarray(res.trend),
    seasonal=np.asarray(res.seasonal),
    remainder=np.asarray(res.resid),
)
fig, axes = P.decomposition_plot(
    dcmp, ["transformed turnover", "trend", "seasonal", "remainder"],
    "STL decomposition of the transformed spine")
P.thin_xticks(axes[-1], n=5)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Transformed spine turnover (yt = Box-Cox of D.spine())
res = STL(yt, period=12, robust=True).fit()
dcmp = spine.assign(
    **{"transformed turnover": yt},
    trend=np.asarray(res.trend),
    seasonal=np.asarray(res.seasonal),
    remainder=np.asarray(res.resid),
)
fig, axes = P.decomposition_plot(
    dcmp, ["transformed turnover", "trend", "seasonal", "remainder"],
    "STL decomposition of the transformed spine")
```

:::

## STL bends where classical decomposition cannot

::: {.incremental}
- **Adaptive**: seasonal pattern can evolve smoothly over time
- **Flexible trend**: estimates non-linear trend curves
- **Outlier-resistant**: unusual spikes do not distort the trend (`robust=True`)
- **Remainder**: isolates pure unexplained variation
:::

::: {.notes}
STL = Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess. Key parameters: period (must provide) and seasonal window.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

# C. Time Series Features {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #9B8EC0)"}

Ch 4 · Summarising thousands of series

## One row per series makes a portfolio tractable

::: {.incremental}
- In practice, you manage **hundreds or thousands** of series
- Manual visual inspection is impossible
- Solution: Compute summary **features** (1 row per series)
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
A **feature** is a numerical summary of a whole series (e.g. trend strength, seasonal strength, entropy).
:::

## Two numbers summarise a whole series

Using STL component variances:

$$F_T = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(T_t + R_t)}\right) \qquad F_S = \max\left(0,\ 1 - \frac{\text{Var}(R_t)}{\text{Var}(S_t + R_t)}\right)$$

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Values fall in **$[0, 1]$**
- **$F_T \approx 0$** $\rightarrow$ No trend | **$F_T \approx 1$** $\rightarrow$ Strong trend
- **$F_S \approx 0$** $\rightarrow$ No seasonality | **$F_S \approx 1$** $\rightarrow$ Strong seasonality
:::


::: {.notes}
Both are one minus a variance ratio. If the remainder is nearly as variable as the
trend plus remainder, the trend is adding nothing and F_T is near zero. If removing
the component barely changes the variance, the component was not there.
:::

## Only seasonal strength separates the portfolio

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9.5
def stl_features(g):
    y = np.log(np.clip(g["y"].to_numpy(), 1e-6, None))
    r = STL(y, period=12, robust=True).fit()
    R, T_, S = np.asarray(r.resid), np.asarray(r.trend), np.asarray(r.seasonal)
    vr = np.var(R)
    return pd.Series({
        "trend_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(T_ + R)),
        "seasonal_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(S + R)),
        "n": len(g),
    })

allr = D.retail_all()
feat = (allr.groupby("unique_id")[["y"]]
             .apply(stl_features, include_groups=False)
             .reset_index())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.3))
lo = feat.nsmallest(1, "seasonal_strength").iloc[0]
hi = feat.nlargest(1, "seasonal_strength").iloc[0]
mine = feat[feat["unique_id"] == D.SPINE_ID].iloc[0]
P.feature_scatter(feat, ax=ax, marks=[(hi, P.ORANGE, "most seasonal"),
                                      (mine, P.BLACK, "the spine"),
                                      (lo, P.PINK, "least seasonal")],
                  title="148 Australian retail series, both axes on the full 0 to 1 scale")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: 148 Australian retail monthly series (allr = D.retail_all())
def stl_features(g):
    y = np.log(np.clip(g["y"].to_numpy(), 1e-6, None))
    r = STL(y, period=12, robust=True).fit()
    R, T_, S = np.asarray(r.resid), np.asarray(r.trend), np.asarray(r.seasonal)
    vr = np.var(R)
    return pd.Series({
        "trend_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(T_ + R)),
        "seasonal_strength": max(0.0, 1 - vr / np.var(S + R)),
    })

allr = D.retail_all()
feat = allr.groupby("unique_id")[["y"]].apply(stl_features, include_groups=False).reset_index()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.3))
P.feature_scatter(feat, ax=ax, marks=[(hi, P.ORANGE, "most seasonal"),
                                      (mine, P.BLACK, "the spine"),
                                      (lo, P.PINK, "least seasonal")],
                  title="148 Australian retail series, both axes on the full 0 to 1 scale")
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Every one of the 148 scores above 0.89 on trend strength and 97% score above 0.96, so trend tells you nothing about which series is which. Seasonal strength runs from 0.26 to 0.98, and that is the axis worth acting on.
:::

## Features route a portfolio to the right model

::: {.incremental}
- **Triage**: focus manual attention on unusual series
- **Model Routing**: skip seasonal models if $F_S \approx 0$
- **Anomaly Detection**: feature outliers often indicate data errors
- **Clustering**: group similar series for global models
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## Golden Rule
When a point looks anomalous in feature space, **always plot the raw series**.
:::
